A1-A2.headline: The Great Gatsby: A Famous American Story

pages.text:
What led F. Scott Fitzgerald to write his most famous novel? Printed in 1925, The Great Gatsby is a sad story set in the American Jazz Age.

It shows the bright energy and fast changes of 1920s Long Island.
pages.caption: The first edition book cover art.

pages.text:
The story takes many real ideas from Fitzgerald's own young life. As a young man, he fell deeply in love with a rich young woman named Ginevra King.

Her wealthy family quickly stopped the match. They felt a poor young man did not have enough money to marry a rich woman from their high circle.

In the book, Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, New York, and lives right next to Jay Gatsby. Gatsby is a quiet, very rich man who holds huge, bright parties every week.

Behind all the music, guests, and lights, he wants only one thing: to win back his old love, Daisy Buchanan.

Famous writers like T. S. Eliot gave the book warm praise right away, yet early sales were very weak. It sold under twenty thousand copies in its first year on store shelves.

That slow start left Fitzgerald feeling deeply sad and worried about his future as a full-time writer.

Fitzgerald's real pain and lost love shaped the sad path of his book's characters. Today, readers all over the world admire the novel.

People praise its sharp look at big money, social class, and wild dreams.

B1-B2.headline: The Real Life Inspirations Behind F. Scott Fitzgerald's Masterpiece

pages.text:
What inspired F. Scott Fitzgerald to write his finest novel? Published in 1925, The Great Gatsby is a tragedy set in the American Jazz Age.

It vividly captures the bright energy and social shifts of 1920s Long Island.

pages.text:
The story draws strongly from Fitzgerald's own early life. As a young man, he fell deeply in love with Ginevra King, a wealthy socialite from a prominent family.

Her parents quickly discouraged the romance, arguing that poor young men lacked the money needed to marry rich women.

In the novel, narrator Nick Carraway moves to West Egg, New York, settling beside Jay Gatsby. A mysterious millionaire, Gatsby throws grand, lively parties every weekend.

Beneath the glittering surface, however, he chases one single dream: winning back his lost love, Daisy Buchanan.

Although literary peers like T. S. Eliot praised the book warmly, its initial release disappointed publishers. It sold fewer than twenty thousand copies during its first year.

Those weak early sales left Fitzgerald deeply discouraged and worried about his writing future.

Fitzgerald's personal setbacks and heartbreak directly shaped his characters' tragic fates. Today, the novel is admired worldwide.

Critics still value its sharp view of wealth, social class, and restless ambition.

C1-C2.headline: Disillusionment and the American Dream in The Great Gatsby

pages.text:
What catalyzed F. Scott Fitzgerald's enduring masterpiece? Published in 1925, The Great Gatsby unfolds as a Jazz Age tragedy.

It acutely illuminates the volatile prosperity and shifting mores of 1920s Long Island.
pages.caption: First edition dust jacket artwork.

imageProvenance.credit: Original cover illustration by Francis Cugat (1893–1981) and published by Charles Scribner's Sons. Digital restoration and enhancement by User:Flask.

pages.text:
The narrative draws substantively upon Fitzgerald's formative romantic disillusionment. During his youth, he courted Ginevra King, an affluent socialite from privileged circles.

Her patrician family decisively thwarted the relationship, insisting that impecunious suitors lacked the financial standing requisite to marry wealthy women.

Within the fiction, narrator Nick Carraway relocates to West Egg, New York, residing adjacent to enigmatic financier Jay Gatsby. Hosting opulent spectacles, Gatsby conceals an unyielding fixation.

His extravagant performance serves one singular purpose: reclaiming his idealized romance with Daisy Buchanan.

Notwithstanding enthusiastic acclaim from literary contemporaries such as T. S. Eliot, the novel faltered commercially upon initial publication. Selling fewer than twenty thousand copies throughout its inaugural year, the book underperformed.

This tepid reception left Fitzgerald despondent and acutely apprehensive regarding his artistic trajectory.

Fitzgerald's personal adversities and romantic disappointments directly forged his protagonists' tragic destiny. Acclaimed globally today, the novel endures.

Scholars prize its trenchant critique of wealth, stratification, and ambition.
